meta.title: The Wired Car
meta.subtitle: How the 40 computers in an Audi e-tron talk to each other, and to you
meta.note: Positions are inferred from each module's role and the MLB evo layout; the car exposes no physical-location data. Harness routes and bus membership are schematic.

buses.label: CAN
buses.why: The workhorse. Multicast with priority arbitration, enough for slow comfort signals.

buses.label: CAN FD
buses.why: CAN extended: bigger payload (up to 64 B) and faster, for dense powertrain and HV traffic.

buses.label: FlexRay
buses.why: Deterministic and redundant: every message has a fixed time slot, so a brake command always arrives in time.

buses.label: LIN
buses.why: One wire, a few cents. For tiny actuators where CAN would be overkill.

buses.label: Automotive Ethernet
buses.why: Bandwidth for camera/radar data, maps and diagnostics. DoIP runs here.

privilegeLadder.name: Session
privilegeLadder.detail: 10 03 opens the extended session. Required for most writes.

privilegeLadder.name: SFD
privilegeLadder.detail: Schutz der Fahrzeugdiagnose (vehicle diagnostics protection). The tester answers a challenge with a token, normally fetched online. This car did not enforce it for the 0x0600 coding write, which succeeded with no 0x27 and no SFD token.
privilegeLadder.blocks: security access, writes, coding, actuator tests (MY2020+), but not the 0x0600 coding write on this car

privilegeLadder.name: Component protection

topology.note: The gateway sits on every bus, so it is never listed as a bus member. FlexRay and Ethernet are drawn as stars centred on the gateway; CAN and CAN FD as shared lines; LIN hangs off its master, not the gateway.

harness.basis: Schematic routing along the usual MLB evo paths: dash cross-car beam, firewall pass-throughs, front-end carrier, sills, centre tunnel, A/B-pillar door boots and the rear wheelhouses. Not traced on the car.

scenarios.title: Select D and pull away
scenarios.blurb: Shift-by-wire, torque requests to both axles, and high-voltage power out of the pack.

steps.caption: The gear selector is just a sensor. It sends a gear request over CAN FD to the Vehicle Control Unit.
The VCU decides how much torque each axle gets and asks the battery for power: three commands on the powertrain CAN FD.
This step is power, with no messages. High-voltage DC leaves the pack, the inverters turn it into 3-phase AC and the motors turn.
The pack reports state of charge back to the VCU, which tells the cluster what to draw as energy flow (BAP), crossing from CAN FD to CAN through the gateway.

scenarios.title: Unlock and open the doors
scenarios.blurb: One body computer commands four door modules, the lamps and the tailgate.

steps.caption: Body Control Module 1 sends lock / window commands to all four door modules on the comfort CAN.
The lights come on to greet the driver. BCM1 drives the Matrix-LED modules over CAN, and BCM2 reaches the rear lights over LIN, the slowest wire in the car.
Opening the tailgate is another BCM1 command on the same CAN.
Finally the cluster is told, over BAP, which doors are open so it can draw them.

scenarios.title: Plug in and charge
scenarios.blurb: The charger, the pack and the thermal system negotiate while the cluster keeps score.

steps.caption: The VCU hands the on-board charger its charge schedule over CAN FD.
Charge power flows into the pack while thermal management asks the BECM to condition the cells. The thermal command crosses from CAN to CAN FD.
The BECM reports state of charge, cell voltages and temperatures; the cluster gets the battery state (BAP).

scenarios.title: Five radars, one picture
scenarios.blurb: Perception runs on Ethernet into the zFAS, which feeds the rest of the car.

steps.caption: The long-range radar and the two front corner radars stream detections over Automotive Ethernet to the zFAS.
The two rear radars do the same. Ethernet is a switched star: every stream passes the switch at the gateway.
The zFAS publishes one fused environment model to the gateway and the assistance status to the cluster.

scenarios.title: A tester reads the cluster
scenarios.blurb: The exact path the inventory scan took: laptop → OBD → gateway → ECU → back.

steps.caption: The laptop opens a DoIP connection (TCP 13400) through the OBD socket. It can only ever talk to the gateway.
The gateway rewrites the logical address and forwards 22 F187 onto the comfort CAN, to the cluster.
The cluster answers 62 F187 4KE920795D; the gateway routes the reply back out. Repeat forty times and you have the inventory.

udsPhases.title: Connect
udsPhases.gist: DoIP to the gateway, then an extended session on the cluster.

udsPhases.title: Identify
udsPhases.gist: Two free reads name the module.

udsTrace.say: The laptop opens a DoIP link on TCP 13400 through the OBD socket. It can only ever talk to the gateway.
Ask the cluster for an extended session. The gateway rewrites the logical address and forwards the request onto CAN.
Read the spare part number. Identification is free and needs no key or token.
Read the ECU name. Repeat these two reads at every address and you have the inventory of all forty modules.

udsTrace.note: this is how all 40 were found

udsTrace.say: Try the coding write. The cluster refuses with 0x24, requestSequenceError, which means something has to happen first.
Write the service-interval parameter F198, in the same extended session.
Write the service date F199. Also accepted.
Retry the coding write, still in the same session. Accepted, then read back to verify. No security access, no SFD token.

udsTrace.meaning: accepted, then read back to verify

secrets.title: The cluster wants two writes before it accepts coding
secrets.secret: The coding write 2E 0600 is refused with 7F 2E 24 (request sequence error) until F198 and F199 have been written in the same extended session. It needs no security access and no SFD token.
secrets.evidence: The exchange in chapter 08, captured live.
secrets.why: No documentation I found mentions this order. Once I knew it, every coding write I needed went through.

secrets.title: The taillight animation is sold as a licence
secrets.secret: The animation is a Functions-on-Demand feature. It needs a licence on the gateway plus one routing bit. The coding alone was not enough.
secrets.evidence: The light package appears as an FS-ID (feature ID) in the gateway's licence list.
secrets.why: The feature was already in the firmware. The car only needed permission to run it.

secrets.title: The car keeps a list of its feature licences
secrets.secret: The gateway holds the car's feature licences as a list, each with a state: locked, unlocked, or unlocked-but-inactive. I read that list to see what the car had.
secrets.evidence: Reading the licence list on the gateway.
secrets.why: It shows the light functions are licensed features, not just coding.

secrets.title: A written licence also has to be activated
secrets.secret: Writing the licence is only half of it; the car also has to be told to activate it. The exact session and routine are part of what I am not publishing.
secrets.why: It explains why a licence write alone is not enough.

secrets.title: The licence list is written as a whole
secrets.secret: The licence list is written as a set, not one entry at a time, so a careless write can drop features the car already owns. The exact mechanism is part of what I am not publishing.
secrets.why: It is why a partial write is risky.

secrets.title: The one finding I am not publishing
secrets.secret: There is a way the car's paid light functions get switched on. I worked out how the licence is written and activated, but I am not describing it here: it is a vendor-signed, paid feature, and I don't want troubles. If you want the feature, buy it from Audi.
secrets.why: This is a teardown of how the car is wired, not a way around the vendor's licensing.

secrets.title: Seven modules reject raw 0x14
secrets.secret: 0x4013 0x4042 0x4044 0x4076 0x407B 0x407C 0x40B8 reject raw UDS 0x14; they need the ODX-defined clear routine.
secrets.evidence: A 0x14 clear probe against every address: 33 accept it, these seven answer serviceNotSupported.
secrets.why: Clearing faults on these modules still requires a bit more work in my custom tool.

secrets.title: A licence write produces a transient DTC storm
secrets.secret: Writing the licence triggers a burst of DTCs with status 0x2E ('all ECUs restarted') until the car settles.
secrets.evidence: The fault read after the licence write: a burst of status-0x2E DTCs that settles.
secrets.why: The burst looks alarming but is expected. Knowing that saved me from chasing faults that were not there.
